beats.intro: Lesson twenty-one. [[sub]]When someone isn't doing the job, is it can't or won't? And what really moves people to work.
beats.cant: A manager's output is the output of the team. [[team]]But a team performs only as well as the people on it. [[two]]When someone is not doing their job, there are only two reasons. [[cant]]They can't do it, or [[wont]]they won't. [[test]]Grove's test: if their life depended on it, could they do it? If yes, it is motivation. If no, it is capability. [[violin]]If his life depended on playing the violin, Grove couldn't. [[mile]]But a mile in six minutes? He probably could. Not that he'd want to.
beats.levers: So a manager has two levers. [[axes]]Picture performance against a person's capability. [[low]]With little motivation, more skill adds only a little. [[high]]With strong motivation, it adds a lot. [[a]]Start at point A. [[train]]Training moves you to the right. [[mot]]Motivation lifts you up, toward point B. [[focus]]This lesson is about the second lever: motivation.
beats.within: How do you motivate someone? Most of us think of doing something to them. [[inside]]Grove says that can't happen. Motivation comes from within. [[env]]All a manager can do is build an environment where motivated people flourish. [[feel]]And the test is performance, not feelings. Someone saying, I feel motivated, means nothing. [[ind]]An attitude can be an indicator, a window into the black box. [[perf]]But the output is better performance at the same level of skill.
beats.fear: For most of history, the motivator was fear. [[dick]]In Dickens' time, no work meant no pay, no pay meant no food, and stealing food could get you hanged. [[know]]Over the thirty years before Grove wrote, gentler approaches took over, perhaps because knowledge workers grew more important. [[manual]]A manual worker's output is easy to measure, and a shortfall shows at once. [[hard]]For a knowledge worker, even the expectations are hard to state. [[galley]]Fear works on galley slaves far better than on computer architects.
beats.maslow: Grove leans on Abraham Maslow, because it matches what he saw at work. [[chain]]Needs create drives, and drives create motivation. [[sat]]But a need that is satisfied stops being a need, and stops motivating. [[keep]]So to keep motivation high, some needs must stay unmet. [[one]]People have many needs at once, but one is strongest, and it sets their performance. [[pyr]]Maslow ranked them. [[up]]When a lower need is met, the next one up takes over.
beats.lower: At the bottom are physiological needs: [[money]]what money buys, like food and clothing. The fear is losing them. [[sec]]Next comes security: protection from slipping back. [[ins]]Medical insurance is the example, so a family isn't bankrupted by hospital bills. [[ben]]Benefits are rarely what drives people. But take them away, and performance would suffer badly.
beats.social: Then the social need: to belong to a group. [[kind]]Not just any group, one like yourself. Happy people seek happy people. And misery loves miserable company. [[friend]]A friend of Grove's went back to a low-paying job after years at home. The money barely helped. She went for the companionship. [[jim]]And Jim, a young engineer, liked his job at a large old company. But his coworkers were married and ten years older, while his roommates at Intel had young friends there. He moved to Intel to belong.
beats.move: As life changes, so does the ruling need. [[chuck]]Chuck, later an Intel manager, began Harvard Business School terrified of flunking out. That is survival. [[study]]Then everyone formed study groups, really to build confidence. That is security. [[section]]Later, his whole class section became a team he was proud of. That is belonging. [[back]]You can slide back down, too. [[quake]]A smooth, motivated team at a California plant felt an earthquake. They dropped wafers, equipment, everything, and ran. Pure survival.
beats.esteem: Those three needs get us to show up. [[perform]]The top two make us perform once we are there. [[jones]]Esteem is keeping up with the Joneses. We frown on that. [[gold]]But if your Jones is last year's Olympic champion, or Laurence Olivier, it is a powerful drive. [[eye]]And esteem is in the eye of the beholder. [[hello]]If the star of your high school team says hello in the hall, you feel terrific. Tell your family, and you get blank stares.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which need is ruling?
beats.limit: Notice something. [[self]]Every need so far is self-limiting. [[met]]Once the goal is reached, the urgency goes. [[vp]]A friend of Grove's was made vice president, a life-long goal. [[crisis]]He was thrown into an early mid-life crisis, looking for something else to drive him.
beats.self: The top of the ladder is self-actualization. [[must]]In Maslow's words: what I can be, I must be. [[best]]A film about athletes put it in its title: Personal Best. Your utter best in a field you chose. [[nolimit]]Here is what makes it special. The other needs switch off once they are met. [[climb]]This one keeps pushing people to higher and higher performance. It has no ceiling.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Can't or won't? Ask: could they, if their life depended on it? [[w2]]Training moves people right; motivation lifts them up. [[w3]]You can't motivate people. You shape their environment. [[w4]]A met need stops motivating; the ruling need can move up or down. [[w5]]Only self-actualization never switches off. Now the lesson practice.
beats.final1: Lesson practice. Five situations from a manager's week.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson twenty-one. Next, how to put the drive to achieve to work.
